_meta.note: Burn-rate projection cases (BEHAVIOR-SPEC sections 3 and 4). Expectations are ported from the Android reference implementation's passing unit tests, so they are proven, not computed by hand. All times are epoch milliseconds; samples are [timestampMs, percent].
_meta.severityNote: Pace severity cases (BEHAVIOR-SPEC section 3.1 — CCM-17 [Pace] on Mac, CCRM-21 on Android). Each case is (usedPct, elapsedMs, windowLengthMs, estimate) -> severity, plus the suppression reason where there is no verdict. estimate is null or an object with hitsLimitAtMs and pctAtReset. Suppression is non-null exactly when severity is 'untracked'. Ported from Android's PaceTest wherever a case exists there.
_meta.tolerance: Floating-point comparisons should allow 0.01 on rates and percents.

estimate.name: steady burn that outruns the window projects a hit before reset
estimate.why: 20%/h observed over two hours with four hours left. 60% remaining at 20%/h hits 100% three hours after the last sample. pctAtReset caps at 100.

estimate.name: slow burn projects the percent at reset instead of a hit
estimate.why: 5%/h with two hours left lands at 30%. The limit is never reached, so hitsLimitAtMs is null rather than a time beyond the reset.

estimate.name: projection is anchored on the latest reading, not the fitted line
estimate.why: Perfectly linear, so the fit passes through the last point: 10%/h with two hours left lands exactly 20 points above the final 40%.

estimate.name: unsorted samples are handled
estimate.why: Input order must not matter — sort before fitting.

estimate.name: least squares ignores an early burst instead of extrapolating it
estimate.why: 30% in the first half hour, then flat for four hours. The endpoints-only slope is 32/4.5 = 7.11%/h; a fit over every point must come out materially shallower. This is why the rate is a least-squares fit and not a first-to-last slope.

estimate.name: too short a span returns null
estimate.why: Only 10 minutes observed, under the 20-minute floor — even though the movement is huge.

estimate.name: flat usage returns null
estimate.why: 0.5 points of movement is under the 1.0-point floor.

estimate.name: single sample returns null
estimate.why: Two points are the minimum for any slope.

estimate.name: a burst then a decline projects nothing
estimate.why: The fitted rate is negative. There is no honest projection to make, so return nothing rather than clamping to zero.

binding.name: tolerance is a quarter of the window
session samples bind despite a drifting resets_at
binding.why: The server slid resets_at forward a minute at a time across these polls. Exact matching would bind only the last point; proximity matching binds all three.

binding.name: the previous window never leaks into the current one
binding.why: A genuine reset moves resets_at by a full window length — four times the tolerance — so the 98% point from the closed window stays out. Without this, a fresh window would inherit the old one's pace.

binding.name: weekly samples bind despite drift and skip missing percents
binding.why: Point 2 has no percent and is skipped rather than counted as zero. Point 4 is last week's window, a full 7 days away, so it stays out.

binding.name: a zero resets_at is never bound
binding.why: Zero means 'window not started', not 'resets at the epoch'. Two zeros must not match each other.

severity.name: 2% four minutes in is untracked, however alarming it projects
severity.why: Android's own example of a meaningless projection (2% after four minutes fits to 150%). Four minutes clears the 3-minute young floor, so the guard that actually catches it is the 5% usage floor — which is why both floors exist and why the reason has to be reported, not just the verdict.

severity.name: real usage in the first minute is still too young
severity.why: Ported from Android. 30 seconds is under the 3-minute session floor.

severity.name: the young floor scales with the period but never drops below a minute
severity.why: A 90-minute window's 1% is 54s, floored to 60s, and 90s clears it. Same inputs as the case above; only the window length differs.

severity.name: a young window outranks even a full one, because carryover looks like this
severity.why: Right after a reset the server can still report the previous window's percent for a poll or two. A one-minute-old window reading 100% is far more likely to be that carryover than a genuinely exhausted window, which is why the two floors are checked ahead of 'spent'.

severity.name: barely-used windows get no verdict, whatever the fit says
severity.why: Three hours into a 7-day window clears the young floor (1% of a week is 1h41m), so what remains is the usage floor: 3% of a window extrapolates to noise. A different sentence from 'too early' is required: a reader shown 'too early' hours into a window would rightly call it a bug.

severity.name: healthy: a projection that lands well inside the limit
close: projected at or above 85% at the reset
the close boundary is inclusive
severity.why: 85.0 exactly is 'cutting it close', not healthy. Two installs disagreeing at the boundary is the bug this pins.

severity.name: running out: the limit lands before the reset
severity.why: Ported from Android. hitsLimitAtMs outranks pctAtReset: a window that runs out early is worse news than one that merely finishes full.

severity.name: spent needs no projection
severity.why: Ported from Android. 99.5 inclusive is the same 'exhausted' line the history bars use. 'Nothing left' needs no forecast to assert.

severity.name: no projection means no verdict about the future
severity.why: A null estimate can never be close or runningOut. Android returns HEALTHY here because their ladder feeds alerts, where both answers mean 'say nothing'; a client that prints copy has to tell the two apart, and either answer alerts identically.
